To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) men's performance-based EI scores, but not their self-reports of EI, are associated with social competence; (b) personality factors are important to consider when examining the role of EI in social functioning; and (c) gender differences in the role of EI are important to consider in research and theory.
self-ratings of emotional intelligence are not as strongly related to social functioning as is performance-based assessment.

(a) the self-ratings of EI are not highly related to performance measures of EI; (b) performance measures of EI are related to real-world social behavior, but self-ratings are not; (c) this pattern holds true only for men; (d) personality traits are important to consider when studying EI; and (e) the MSCEIT may be a better measure of EI than self-ratings.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether emotional abilities (assessable with performance measures) are related to social competence (measured with self-reports).

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the MSCEIT and self-report EI measures are measuring different things and that the two measures should be used together in research and practice.
EI is not a unitary concept and that the self-report and performance aspects of EI are not necessarily correlated with each other and may have differential relations with social functioning.
EI, as measured by the MSCEIT, is not a good predictor of social functioning.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ability-based approach to EI is a useful framework for understanding social functioning, and it is particularly important to include performance-based measures of EI.
the MSCEIT is a better measure of EI than self-ratings and that the MSCEET may be a better predictor of real-time social functioning for men.
EI is a multidimensional construct that is important to social functioning and that it may be best to assess EI with multiple measures.
The main takeaway from our work is that
emotional abilities may be important for social functioning, but the way they contribute may be different for men and women.
emotional intelligence is a complex construct and that the way in which it is measured is crucial.
self-report and performance assessments of emotional abilities may not be measuring the same construct.
